newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire airline adopts Alliance name as rebels recruit.
newsitem.headline: Zaire airline adopts Alliance name as rebels recruit.

text.p: Sign-writers have painted out the old Zaire Airlines billboards in Lubumbashi and replaced them with a logo honouring rebels who are acquiring emblems of state as quickly as they capture territory.

With their leader, Laurent Kabila, temporarily resident in Zaire's second city along with his ministers, Lubumbashi has become the de facto capital of the armed movement that is closing in on Kinshasa to topple President Mobutu Sese Seko.
The rebels say it won't be for long: they confidently expect to be in Kinshasa within weeks, maybe sooner.

Meanwhile in the capital of the country's richest province -- an area the size of France -- rebel officials do business with executives from international mining companies and at the same time recruit teenagers clamouring to join the cause.

The red, yellow and blue logo AAL appeared on three billboards on the road from Lubumbashi to the city airport, which controllers said was busier now than before it was taken over by rebel forces two weeks ago.

The success of Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL) has apparently persuaded Zaire Airlines and the local Shabair to get together and rename their private operation Alliance Airlines (AAL).
Their slogan and phone numbers remained unchanged.
The airport was open to scheduled flights, and there was no shortage of planes taking off and landing, ferrying troops and new recruits around the half of Zaire controlled by the AFDL.

The smart executive jets of a couple of major mineral firms stood parked on the apron and a white, aeronautically stylish Buffalo transport plane belonging to an international construction firm taxied out carrying equipment.
The AFDL has already signed one big minerals exploitation deal since taking over in Shaba province, where deposits of copper, cobalt and zinc are described as fabulously rich.
And it looks certain to write more business before the month is out, although the government maintains the rebels' $1.0 billion deal with America Mineral Fields Inc contravened international law.

In the provincial capital, a throng of excited youths gathers daily outside the AFDL's recruiting office to sign up with the rebel army for what Kabila promises to be the final push, on to the capital Kinshasa "before June".

"It's been a spontaneous process. They've been coming in since the Alliance took over. But after Kabila's rally on Saturday there's been a stream," said Colonel Muchail N'Tambo Rindachi, the local AFDL recruiting officer.

Kabila told a crowd of 10,000 at a football stadium outside the city on Saturday that he wanted all the young men of Shaba to join up and help the rebel army march into the tense capital and finish the job of toppling the Mobutu regime.

"We've had over 2,000 recruited so far. We're spreading out the operation to other towns including Kolwezi this week," Rindachi said. "There were just too many of them to handle today. They were squashed against the walls," he added, gesturing in the direction of a shady courtyard.

The colonel said boys as young as 14 and 15 were being recruited, if they were judged fit. Besides frontline duties the Alliance also had to act as police in captured towns, to patrol roads and maintain public order, he said.
On the potholed roads of the city, trucks laden with recruits rumble out to the airport or up to the elegant old railway station for the four day train trip up country to their training grounds.
